newsitem.title: FRANCE: Consolidation seen big theme at Paris air show.
newsitem.headline: Consolidation seen big theme at Paris air show.

text.p: Talk of mergers and privatisations will likely hold sway when the world's aerospace industry gets together at the Paris Air Show, which opens next Saturday.

For a week the Le Bourget business airport on the northern Paris suburb will heave with visiting ministers, delegations, and aerospace executives, brought together by the prospect of order contracts and corporate deals.
And the thrill-seeking public will come in thousands, attracted by the roar of jet engines passing a few hundred feet overhead and the smell of high-grade kerosene in the air.

But the business issues are clear. While U.S. firms race ahead in megamergers to form powerful combinations aimed at squeezing the last dollar out of thinning defence and research budgets, European companies are only groping towards a concept of integration of their military and civil activities.

France's Aerospatiale, British Aerospace Plc (BAe), Germany's Daimler-Benz Aerospace (Dasa) and Casa of Spain last month agreed to create a single company at the European level to manage all their space, civil and defence interests, Aerospatiale chairman Yves Michot said.

That integrated management of national programmes was Europe's best hope of confronting the massive concentration of defence and military power taking place in the United States, he told journalists at a seminar in Grasse, southern France.
"We can't settle for (restructuring) civil aeronautics, we have to go further than that, we have to talk about all our activities," he said.

"The scheme allows companies with their programmes to come together, to have complete responsibility for programmes, use the resources of national companies, and allow them to continue to control their own assets," he added.

So far, the four European companies have focused converting the Airbus Industrie passenger plane consortium into a limited liability company by 1999, to boost competitiveness in the face of the Boeing /McDonnell Douglas merger.

A first step in the new accord would make Airbus into a single corporate entity, give it a project management mission and allow it to hold on to money which it currently passes onto its four industrial partners.
Other issues vital to European consolidation are the proposed merger between combat plane maker Dassault Aviation and Aerospatiale and the privatisation of defence electronics Thomson-CSF.

The previous French conservative government had planned to announce terms of the Dassault/Aerospatiale merger at the Air Show, in which Dassault was expected to hold around 20 percent of the merged group.
The arrival of a new French Socialist government, with Communist ministers, has cast doubt over those corporate deals.
President Jacques Chirac opens the show and the new Prime Minister, Lionel Jospin, gives a keynote speech on June 22.

While France hesitates, a $14 billion merger between undisputed leader in passenger jets Boeing and military specialist McDonnell Douglas is nearing the end of regulatory scrutiny. The European Commission's anti-trust probe is due to rule on the deal by July 31.
Also on the starting block is a $9.5 billion merger between U.S. missile giants Raytheon Co and Hughes Electronics Corp.
While competition between U.S. and European majors continues unababted, emerging players are also looking for a share of world markets.

Of the 42 countries attending the show and 1,760 exhibitors, the Moldova republic will make its debut, while Denel of South Africa and IPTN of Indonesia are making big efforts to enter the global scene. The CIS republics will also be in force.
Some 220 aircraft will be on show, on the ground and in flying displays, with 15 coming from the United States.
